Board cards use the catalog's four a1e05 concept ids (attention, transformers-as-intuition, context-windows, position); strings reach back to tokens (a1e03), embeddings (a1e04) and neural-network (a1e02), and ahead to next-token-prediction (a1e06), chunking (a3e02) and statelessness (a1e09)
title: Paying Attention
setting: a switchboard where every line listens to every other

post.author: u/ringdown_gwilym
post.title: I rewired an old switchboard so every line listens to every other. At 2:14 AM it told me a man who died in 1983 would ring me back.

blocks.text: I'm a junior developer, and on weekends I volunteer at a telephone museum in our town's old exchange. For the night opening I built an exhibit on the 1950s switchboard in the operators' room. You type a message, and each word takes one line on the board, in order. The board has 8 lines.

Behind each word I set three cards of numbers by hand: what the word is looking for, what it offers as a label, and what it passes on. For every line, my program scores every line on the board, its own included, by how well what it's looking for fits each label. It turns the scores into shares that add up to 1, lights one lamp per share, brighter for bigger, then mixes what each line passes on, in those shares. Eight lines listening to eight lines: 64 lamps.
Every line also hums at its own pitch. Before I added the hums, *the dog bit the postman* and *the postman bit the dog* lit exactly the same lamps, only shuffled. It couldn't hear who bit whom.
The trick for visitors: type a sentence with *she* in it, and the board pulls a cord from *she* to the line whose lamp burns brightest. In rehearsals it never missed.

On Saturday, after we closed, I stayed to pack up. At 2:14 the exhibit phone rang. An old woman, very polite, asked me to tell Ewart that Miss Clemency had rung and that she would ring back. I typed it the way the old operators wrote their slips:

slip    miss clemency rang for ewart said she would ring back
        10 words   board: 8 lines
board   rang for ewart said she would ring back
cord    she -> ewart   0.28
print   EWART WILL RING BACK

There's a brass plate on the chair at position one that nobody polishes: E. QUILLIAM, NIGHTS, 1961 TO 1979. The history wall says Ewart Quilliam ran the night board here for eighteen years. He died in 1983.
The board never heard her name.
At four I ran the same ten words through the copy of the program on my laptop, set to 10 lines. The cord went from *she* to Clemency, 0.74. *miss* got 0.13. Ewart got 0.02.
We open again next Saturday, and the museum wants visitors to leave longer messages on the exhibit phone. What did the board do with her message? And what do I change before then?

Her slip, 10 words starting miss clemency rang, goes to the board with 8 lines and 64 lamps, which takes only the newest 8 words, rang for ewart said she would ring back. The first two words, miss and clemency, never get a line. On the board, the brightest lamp for she is ewart, 0.28. The same slip goes whole to the laptop copy with 10 lines and 100 lamps, where the brightest lamp for she is clemency, 0.74, with miss at 0.13 and ewart at 0.02.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: That's a cold thing to read at 2 AM, and nothing on that board is haunted. You built what engineers call attention, the core of the models behind chat assistants. Each word is a token; real tokenizers cut some words into pieces, but on your board every word is one. Your three cards have names. The query is what a token is looking for, the key is the label it offers, and the value is what it passes on. A token's score for another is how well its query fits that one's key. A step called softmax turns a row of scores into attention weights, positive shares that add up to 1, and the token's output is the values mixed by those weights. When every token in a text does this with every other, it's self-attention, and your grid of lamps, one row per listener, is what people draw as a heat map. The hums are position information. The 8 lines are the board's context window: the most tokens it can attend to at once. Two questions. Count the words on the slip and the lines on the board: which words never got a lamp? And look at the brightest lamp in each run, 0.74 and 0.28. What would the board have to light to tell you the name it wanted wasn't there?

replies.author: u/ringdown_gwilym
replies.text: Found it. Line 41 of my program: if a message is longer than the board, keep the newest 8 words. I wrote it in June so a long message couldn't crash the exhibit, and forgot. *miss clemency* never reached a line. And there's no lamp for nobody. Every row adds up to 1, so something always burns brightest.

comments.author: u/day_board_oonagh
comments.text: I worked a cord board for eleven years, days, in the seventies. The night operators kept slips just the way you typed hers, and our supervisor had one rule for a caller who rambled: write the name first, before anything else, because once they've hung up the name is the one thing you can't ask for again.

comments.author: u/longdoc_lauritz
comments.text: Something like this cost my team a month. Our tool summarized contracts with a language model, and for long contracts the summaries were fluent, confident and quietly about the second half only. The definitions were all on page one. Nobody saw an error, because there wasn't one.

reply.prompt: The museum opens again next Saturday, and longer messages are coming. What should Gwilym change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Retune the cards so *she* pulls much harder toward women's names. With a stronger pull, the cord can't land on a man like Ewart, even when the start of a message is cut.
options.verdict: No setting reaches a missing word
options.part2: I tripled the pull on *she*'s query card toward women's names and typed Clemency's slip in again. Ewart's lamp went dim. The brightest lamp for *she* moved to *rang*, a word that isn't a person at all, and the board printed RANG WILL RING BACK. On Saturday a man left a long message for his sister, and the board lost her name the same way. No card on the board can pull toward a word that never got a line.
options.senior: Attention can only weigh the tokens inside its window. Retuning changes how the weights are shared among what is there; it can't bring back words that were cut before the model saw them. Fix what goes in, not how it is weighed.

options.text: Change line 41 to keep the first 8 words instead of the newest 8. Callers say their names first, so the name will always be on the board for *she* to find.
options.verdict: A silent cut at the other end
options.part2: Clemency's slip came out right: the board kept miss clemency rang for ewart said she would, and the cord went to Clemency. Then on Saturday a woman left a message for the curator with her phone number at the end. The board kept her first 8 words and printed a slip with no number on it, and nothing anywhere said anything was missing. She rang the museum on Monday, not pleased.
options.senior: Keeping the start instead of the end only moves the loss, and the program still throws words away without telling anyone. Which part matters changes from message to message. Check the length first, and decide in the open what happens when it doesn't fit.

options.text: Rebuild the board with 40 lines before Saturday, so even long messages fit whole. Every word gets a line, so *she* always has the right name to listen to.
options.verdict: Trade-off: it fits, at 25 times the lamps
options.part2: Forty lines listening to forty lines is 1,600 lamps, 25 times the 64 I have, because every line listens to every other. By Saturday I'd wired 20 lines, 400 lamps, and it took both evenings. Clemency's slip fit and the cord found her. Then a boy read a whole poem into the phone, 63 words, and line 41 kept the newest 20 without a word to anyone.
options.senior: A bigger window really helps, which is why providers keep making them bigger. But attention compares every token with every other, so the work grows with the square of the length, and there is always a longer input. Size the window for real traffic, and still decide what happens past it.

options.text: Count the words of every message before it goes on the board. Over 8, cut nothing silently: print the slip as too long, keep the whole message for a person, and tally it.
options.part2: I put a counter in front of the board. Saturday brought 31 messages. 6 were longer than 8 words, and each printed TOO LONG, SEE BOOK and went into the visitors' book in full. At 2:14 on Sunday morning the exhibit phone rang again. Clemency Tregarthen, 87, who worked the day board here until 1966. She'd heard the old night number read out in the radio advert for our opening and wondered if Ewart still answered it. I read her the history wall. She was quiet for a long time, then thanked me for taking such a careful message.
options.senior: Count tokens against the window before you send. When an input doesn't fit, choose on purpose: refuse it with a clear message, pass it to a person, shorten it or split it, and never trim silently. Then count how often it happens, because that tells you whether a bigger window is worth paying for.

sim.title: Wire the board yourself
sim.lede: You're Gwilym at four in the morning with the laptop copy of the board. The message is Clemency's slip, ten words, one token per word. Every word has three hand-set cards of 3 numbers each, its query, key and value: a teaching simplification, since real models learn their numbers, and far more of them. Pick a listening word to see its row of lamps, its attention weights over every word on the board, which always add up to 1. The grid under it is the whole heat map, one row per listener, and under that is every word's output, its values mixed by its weights. The position switch adds each line's hum, its position information, to all three cards. Shuffle rearranges the words on the board. The lines slider is the context window, from 4 to 10: like line 41, the program keeps the newest words and marks the rest cut.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start where Saturday was, 8 lines, hums on, *she* listening. *miss* and *clemency* are marked cut, never on the board, and the brightest lamp is Ewart's, 0.28. Slide to 10: the brightest lamp jumps to Clemency, 0.74, with *miss* at 0.13 and Ewart at 0.02. Slide to 9: *miss* is gone but Clemency stays, at 0.78. Back to 8 and Clemency is gone again. Now slide down to 4: *she would ring back* is all that's left, and the biggest share, 0.38, goes to *she* itself. Something always wins. Then set 10 lines, turn the hums off and press Shuffle: every word's output is the same three numbers as before, in a new order. Turn the hums on and shuffle again: the outputs change.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the board is haunted. Gwilym built one attention head: every word scores every word on the board, turns the scores into weights that add up to 1, and mixes what they pass on. His program cut the first two words to fit 8 lines, so *she* gave its biggest weight to the best match left: Ewart.

steps.title: Attention: each word decides how much to listen to every other.
steps.text: For each token, attention scores every token in view, itself included, by how relevant it looks. Softmax turns that row of scores into weights: each one positive, all of them adding up to 1, with the biggest score getting by far the biggest share. The token's output is the others' information mixed in those proportions. On the laptop copy, *she* gave 0.74 of its attention to Clemency, 0.13 to *miss* and 0.02 to Ewart, so the output for *she* is mostly Clemency's information: after one step of attention, the numbers for *she* carry who she is. Vaswani and colleagues, who introduced the Transformer in 2017, describe the output as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key. An attention weight is not a neuron's weight from case 2. It is worked out fresh for every text, while a neuron's weights are learned once, in training.

steps.title: Query, key and value: looking for, label, passing on.
steps.text: Each token brings three lists of numbers. The query is what it is looking for. The key is the label it offers to everyone else's queries. The value is what it hands to whoever listens. A token's score for another is how well its query fits the other's key: multiply the two lists number by number and add up. The paper also divides each score by the square root of the key's length, so long lists don't make the scores huge. Keeping label and content apart is the point: Clemency's key says a person, a woman, which is what *she* is looking for, and her value is what *she* receives. Gwilym set his 30 cards by hand. In a real model nobody does: each token's embedding is multiplied by learned weights to make its query, key and value, and training adjusts those weights. The 2017 Transformer used vectors of 512 numbers per token, with 64-number queries and keys.

steps.title: Distant words meet in one step, and a transformer stacks it.
steps.text: *she* and *clemency* sit five words apart, and attention links them in one step, as easily as neighbours. Older models read a text one token at a time, so a link had to be carried along word by word. Vaswani's paper says a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, and that the shorter these paths, the easier long-range dependencies are to learn. One attention head looks for one kind of thing. A real model runs several heads side by side, each with its own queries, keys and values, so one can track who *she* is while another tracks which verb goes with which noun. Their outputs are combined, and then each token passes through a small neural network like the ones in case 2. That pair is one layer, and a transformer is a stack of these layers: the 2017 one had 6, with 8 heads each. Gwilym's board is one head of one layer.

steps.title: Position: attention on its own can't hear order.
steps.text: Nothing in a score depends on where a word sits. Shuffle the words and every token gets exactly the same weights and the same output as before, only in a new order, which is why *the dog bit the postman* and *the postman bit the dog* lit the same lamps. So position information is added to each token before attention runs. The paper puts it plainly: in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. Its version adds sine and cosine waves of different frequencies to each token's embedding. It also tried positions learned in training and found the two versions produced nearly identical results. Gwilym's hums are the same idea in miniature: three small numbers per line, made from a fast wave and a slow one, added to all three cards. With them on, shuffling changes the outputs, because a word in a different slot carries a different hum.

steps.title: The context window: what isn't on the board doesn't exist.
steps.text: A model can attend to a fixed number of tokens at once: its context window. Gwilym's is 8. Anthropic's documentation defines the context window as all the text a language model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself, so instructions, earlier turns and the answer all share it. What happens to text past it depends on the application. Gwilym's program kept the newest 8 words, silently. Anthropic's API returns an error saying the prompt is too long when the input alone exceeds the window, and its docs note that chat interfaces can manage the window on a rolling first in, first out basis. Either way the model never sees what didn't fit, and attention can't flag a gap: the weights always add up to 1 over whatever is there, so *she* lit Ewart at 0.28 rather than nothing. And because every token is compared with every other, the work grows with the square of the length: 8 lines need 64 lamps, 40 would need 1,600. Case 6 shows how a stack of these layers ends in next-token prediction: choosing the next token, one at a time.

diagram.aria: One step of attention for the word she on the laptop copy, all 10 words in view. She's query, looking for a person, a woman, is compared with every key. Clemency's key, a person, a woman, fits best. Miss's key, a woman's title, fits partly. The other 8 keys, including Ewart's, a man, fit poorly. Softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to 1: 0.74 for Clemency, 0.13 for miss and 0.13 for the other 8 together, Ewart 0.02 of it. She's output is the values mixed by those weights, so it is mostly Clemency. Each slot's hum is added to every card first, and only words on the board take part.

notes.text: each slot's hum is added to every card first
only words on the board take part

explain.caption: Read left to right. *she*'s query is compared with every key on the board, its own included. Clemency's key fits best, *miss*'s partly, the other 8 poorly, Ewart's among them at 0.02. Softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to 1: 0.74, 0.13 and 0.13 for the other 8 together. *she*'s output is everyone's values mixed by those weights, so it is mostly Clemency. On the 8-line board, Clemency's key was never there to compare.

fix.title: The fix: count before the board, and never cut silently
fix.text: Check the length before anything reaches the model. Count the tokens of everything you send, instructions included, with the provider's token counter for that model, and compare the total with its context window, leaving room for the answer. Anthropic's docs point to their token counting API for exactly this. When something doesn't fit, decide on purpose and make the decision visible. You can refuse it with a clear message, as Anthropic's API does when the input alone is too long. You can hand it to a person, as Gwilym's TOO LONG slip does. You can shorten it, split it into pieces that each fit and combine the results, or look up only the parts that matter: Season 3 builds that kind of retrieval and chunking properly. You can move to a model with a bigger window. What you never do is trim silently, because a silent trim looks exactly like a correct answer. Log every overflow, so you know how often it happens and whether a bigger window is worth paying for.

limits: Counting tells you a message won't fit, not which part of it matters. Shortening or splitting can still separate *she* from *clemency*: a piece that starts at *rang* has the board's problem all over again. Splits have to carry the names and facts each piece depends on.

A bigger window isn't free, and it isn't perfect. Attention compares every token with every other, so the work climbs fast with length, and Anthropic's docs warn that as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, which they call context rot. Case 9 looks at long contexts.

Everything in a request shares the window: the instructions, the earlier turns of a conversation and the answer being written. A message that fits on its own can stop fitting once the rest is added, so count the whole request.

Short window (8 lines here)

Long messages, letters, documents and long conversations, whole.

explain.seniorTake: Treat the context window as a budget counted in tokens and shared by everything in the request: instructions, history, documents and the answer. Count before you send, decide on purpose what happens when it doesn't fit, and make that decision visible, never a silent trim. And remember that attention can only weigh what reached it: no tuning of the weights brings back a token that was cut.

realWorld.title: The Transformer, 2017
realWorld.text: In Attention Is All You Need, Ashish Vaswani and seven co-authors proposed the Transformer, a network built on attention without the step-by-step reading earlier translation models relied on. They describe an attention function as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, computed as a weighted sum of the values, with each weight coming from how well the query fits the corresponding key. Their version scores with the query and key multiplied number by number and added up, divides each score by the square root of the key length, and applies a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values. The base model works with vectors of 512 numbers, runs 8 attention heads with 64-number queries and keys, and stacks 6 identical layers, each with a self-attention step and a small network applied to every position separately.

realWorld.title: Order has to be added
realWorld.text: The same paper explains why the Transformer needs position information: in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. It adds positional encodings to the input embeddings, using sine and cosine functions of different frequencies. The authors also experimented with learned positional embeddings and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results, and chose the sine version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.

realWorld.title: Heads that find what *its* refers to
realWorld.text: The paper notes that a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, and that the shorter the paths between positions, the easier long-range dependencies are to learn. Its pictures of trained attention show it working. One figure shows two attention heads in layer 5 of 6, apparently involved in anaphora resolution, with the attentions from the word *its* marked as very sharp. Another shows many heads following a distant dependency of the verb *making*, completing the phrase *making...more difficult*. For very long sequences, it suggests self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r around each position, to cut the work.

realWorld.title: Where attention started
realWorld.text: Three years earlier, Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio were working on neural machine translation, where one network read a whole source sentence into a single fixed-length vector and another wrote the translation from it. They conjectured that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck, and let the model automatically (soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word. That soft search, a set of weights over the source words recomputed for every word written, is the attention the Transformer later built everything on. The paper was accepted at ICLR 2015.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: what a context window holds, and what happens past it
realWorld.text: Anthropic's documentation defines the context window as all the text a language model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself, and calls it a working memory. When this case was written, the page listed windows of up to 1M tokens, depending on the model, and 200k tokens for other models, including Claude Sonnet 4.5. Everything counts toward it: the instructions, every message and the output. If the input alone already exceeds the window, the API returns an error, prompt is too long, on every model, while chat interfaces such as claude.ai can also manage the context window on a rolling first in, first out basis. The page also warns that more context isn't automatically better: as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot. To stay within the limits, it recommends the token counting API to estimate usage before sending.

asked: Why do transformers need position information?
What is a context window, and what do you do when your input is longer?
interview.answer: Attention lets every token decide how much to listen to every other token in its context. Each token has a query, what it's looking for, a key, the label it offers, and a value, what it passes on. A token scores every key against its query, softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to 1, and the token's new vector is the values mixed by those weights, so a pronoun can pull in the meaning of a name several words back in one step. A transformer stacks layers of this, with several heads per layer looking for different things, each layer followed by a small neural network. Position: the scores don't depend on where a token sits, so without position information a shuffled sentence gives the same outputs in a shuffled order, and the dog bit the postman reads like the postman bit the dog. So position information, sine waves in the original paper or positions learned in training, is added to each token's vector. The context window is the most tokens a model can attend to at once, counting the instructions, the history and the answer. When my input is longer, I count tokens before sending and choose on purpose: retrieve only the relevant parts, or split the input into chunks and combine the results, which is retrieval and chunking (Season 3); summarize older material; use a model with a bigger window, which costs more and can lose accuracy as it fills; or refuse with a clear error. Never trim silently, because nothing downstream will notice. And since a model keeps nothing between requests, its statelessness, the window is also its only memory, which is case 9's subject.

terms.def: A step inside a model where each token scores how relevant every other token in view is, turns the scores into weights that add up to 1, and mixes the others' information by those weights.
Attention where every token in a text attends to every token of the same text, itself included. Gwilym's board does self-attention.
In attention, a token's list of numbers for what it is looking for. Gwilym's first card on each line.
In attention, a token's list of numbers for the label it offers to other tokens' queries. Gwilym's second card.
In attention, a token's list of numbers for what it passes on to whoever listens. Gwilym's third card.
In attention, how well one token's query fits another token's key: the two lists multiplied number by number and added up. Bigger means more relevant.
A step that turns any row of scores into positive weights that add up to 1, giving the biggest score by far the biggest share. It never gives a weight of exactly 0.
One token's share of another token's attention, between 0 and 1. A row of them adds up to 1. Not the same as a neuron's weight in case 2, which is learned in training.
In attention, a token's new list of numbers: every value in view, mixed by that token's attention weights.
A grid of numbers drawn as brightness. Gwilym's lamp grid is one: a row per listening token, a column per token listened to.
One attention step with its own queries, keys and values. A model runs several side by side, each free to look for a different kind of link. Gwilym's board is one head.
A model built from a stack of layers, each with attention heads followed by a small neural network for every token. Introduced by Vaswani and colleagues in 2017.
Numbers added to each token that say where it sits, so attention can tell word order. Also called positional encoding. Gwilym's hums.
The paper's name for position information: numbers added to each token's embedding, made from sine and cosine waves or learned in training.
This case's name for the position information on Gwilym's board: three small numbers per line, made from a fast wave and a slow one.
A smooth wave that rises and falls between -1 and 1. A cosine wave is the same wave shifted. Mixing waves of different speeds gives each position its own pattern.
The fixed number of tokens a model can attend to at once, counting everything you send and, for many models, the answer it writes. Gwilym's board has a window of 8.
Input that doesn't fit in the context window. The application decides what happens to it: an error, a cut, a split.
Cutting tokens off an input so it fits the window. Silent trimming is the dangerous kind: nobody is told anything was cut.
A rule where the oldest item leaves first. A chat that manages its window this way drops the oldest turns as new ones arrive.
Anthropic's name for accuracy and recall getting worse as the number of tokens in the context grows.
Here, how often a model's answers are right, and how much of the relevant information in its context it actually finds and uses.
What something can hold and use right now. Anthropic's docs describe the context window as a model's working memory.
Twice the length means four times the work. Attention compares every token with every other, so 8 tokens need 64 comparisons and 40 need 1,600.
A short word that stands in for a name, like she, he, it or its.
Working out what a word like she or its refers to. The 2017 paper shows attention heads that seem to do it.
A link between words that sit far apart in a text, like a pronoun and the name it stands for.
The paper's phrase for how a query is compared with a key to give a score.
A list with the same number of numbers however long the text was. Squeezing a whole sentence into one was the problem attention was invented to get around.
A narrow point that limits everything after it, like the neck of a bottle.
Translating text from one language to another with a neural network. Attention was first built for it.
Looking up only the parts of a large body of text that matter for a question, and sending just those to the model. Season 3 builds it.
Splitting a long text into pieces that each fit the window, so they can be processed or looked up separately. Season 3 covers it.
A model keeping nothing between requests. Whatever it should know has to be sent again each time, inside the window. Case 9 covers it.
What a language model does with all this: score every token in its vocabulary as the next one and pick one. Case 6 covers it.
A provider's endpoint that counts a request's tokens for a given model before you send it.
An app where you talk with a language model in turns, like a conversation.
International Conference on Learning Representations, one of the main yearly research conferences in machine learning.
A panel where telephone operators connected callers by hand, plugging cords between sockets, with a small lamp for each line.
The building where a town's telephone lines met and were connected to each other, by operators at switchboards before machines took over.
The person at a switchboard who answered calls, connected them and took messages.
On a switchboard, a cable with a plug at each end, used to connect one line to another.
A short written note of a phone message: who rang, for whom, and what they said.

atWork: Pick one feature at work that sends text to a language model: a summarizer, a chat assistant, a document question box. Look up the context window of the model it really uses in the provider's docs. Then find the code path for a long input. Does anything count tokens before sending? When the input is too long, what happens: an error, a trim (and from which end), a split? Try it: send the longest real input you can find, with the full instructions, and check whether the answer uses something from the very start. If the app trims silently, add a count before sending, log every overflow, and decide with your team what should happen instead, so the next long document doesn't lose its first page without anyone noticing.

recall.prompt: Your team's meeting-notes tool works well on short meetings. For a two-hour meeting, its notes cover only the last hour and never mention decisions made at the start. Nothing in the logs looks wrong. What do you suspect, and what do you check and change?

keyIdeas.idea: The transcript is longer than the context window, and something cuts it to fit without saying so
Count the tokens of the whole request, instructions included, against the model's window
Handle long input on purpose: split it into parts and combine, retrieve what matters, or use a bigger window
Make overflow visible instead of silent, and test with long inputs

recall.model: I'd suspect the transcript is longer than the model's context window and the app trims it to fit, keeping the end, so the model never sees the first hour. Nothing looks wrong because a silent trim produces a fluent answer, not an error. I'd count the tokens of the whole request, instructions plus transcript plus room for the notes, against the window of the model we use, and find the code that trims. Then I'd handle long meetings on purpose: split the transcript into parts that fit, take notes on each and combine them, or move to a model with a bigger window if the cost is worth it. And I'd make overflow visible, with a warning on the notes, and add a two-hour meeting to our tests.

recall.prompt: On the 8-line board, why did the brightest lamp for *she* go to Ewart?
options: Ewart's key fitted the query for *she* better than Clemency's did
The hums made whichever name sat nearest to *she* win
The weights always add up to 1, and Ewart was the best fit left
Softmax picks a token at random when the scores are close
recall.why: Clemency was never on the board, so she had no lamp at all. Softmax shares a total of 1 over whatever is in view, so something always burns brightest: Ewart, a person, fitted best of what was left, at a dim 0.28. With all 10 words in view, Clemency gets 0.74 and Ewart 0.02.

recall.prompt: Explain to a new teammate, in plain words, what attention does for one token, using query, key and value.

keyIdeas.idea: The token scores every token in view by how well each key fits its query
Softmax turns the scores into weights that are positive and add up to 1
Its output is the values mixed by those weights
Every token does this with every other, so distant words connect in one step

recall.model: For one token, attention asks how much to listen to each token in view, itself included. The token's query says what it's looking for; every token offers a key, its label, and a value, what it passes on. The token scores each key by how well it fits its query, softmax turns those scores into weights that are all positive and add up to 1, and the token's output is everyone's values mixed in those proportions. So *she* can take most of its new meaning from a name several words back, in one step, and every token does this at once with every other.

recall.prompt: Why does a transformer need position information?
options: Without it, shuffling the words would only shuffle the outputs
Without it, a row of attention weights wouldn't add up to 1
It tells the model how many tokens fit in its context window
It makes distant words count for less than nearby words do
recall.why: Nothing in an attention score depends on where a token sits, so shuffling the words only shuffles the outputs: *the dog bit the postman* and *the postman bit the dog* look alike. Adding position information to each token lets the scores and outputs depend on order. How much near or far words matter is learned, not set by it.

recall.prompt: Your app's input is longer than the model's context window. What happens to the extra text?
options: The model reads it more slowly, in a second pass
It depends on the application; the model never sees it
The model squeezes it into the window by itself
The model keeps the first and last parts and skips the middle
recall.why: The window is a hard limit on what the model can attend to. What happens past it is up to the software around the model: Gwilym's program kept the newest 8 words, Anthropic's API returns an error when the input alone is too long, and its docs note that chat interfaces can drop the oldest turns first. Find out which one your stack does.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The board is a permanent exhibit now, and my day job pulled me onto something real: a tool that reads the transcripts of callers' voicemails and drafts a reply with a hosted language model. My teammate Radomir wrote the first version. It sends a page of instructions plus the transcript, and so that long calls never crash it, it keeps the newest part of the transcript that fits. Customers with long calls started getting replies that answered only the end of the call, often addressed to the wrong person, since callers give their names first. Radomir wants to switch to a model with a window four times bigger and delete the trimming code, since everything will fit.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What went wrong, and what would you tell Radomir?

keyIdeas.idea: The app cuts the start of long transcripts without telling anyone, so the model never sees the opening
A bigger window helps but costs more, still has a limit, and very long inputs can lose accuracy
Count tokens before sending and handle overflow on purpose, keeping the caller's details with whatever is sent, and log it

coldCase.model: The code is trimming silently: when a call is too long it keeps the end, so the model never sees the opening, where the caller gives their name, and it answers the part it can see, addressed to whoever is named there. A model with a bigger window would help, but it costs more per request, attention's work grows fast with length, accuracy and recall degrade on very long inputs, and some calls will still be longer. So keep a check, not a trim: count the tokens of the instructions plus the transcript before sending, against the window with room for the reply. When it doesn't fit, handle it on purpose: summarize or split the transcript and combine the results, always carrying the caller's name and key facts along, or flag it for a person. Log every overflow so we know how often it happens, and only then decide whether the bigger model is worth it.

sources.title: Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser and Polosukhin, Attention Is All You Need, NIPS 2017 (arXiv 1706.03762): the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms; an attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, a weighted sum of the values with weights from a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key; dot products divided by the square root of dk, then a softmax; dmodel 512, h = 8 heads, dk = dv = 64; N = 6 identical layers of multi-head self-attention plus a position-wise feed-forward network; positional encodings added to the input embeddings, sine and cosine functions of different frequencies; learned positional embeddings gave nearly identical results; a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations; restriction to a neighborhood of size r for very long sequences; figure 4, two heads in layer 5 of 6 apparently involved in anaphora resolution, very sharp attentions for the word its; figure 3, the verb making and making...more difficult

Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio, Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate (arXiv 1409.0473, first posted September 2014, accepted at ICLR 2015 as an oral presentation): the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck; a model that can automatically (soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word

Anthropic, Context windows (Claude Platform docs): all the text a language model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself; a working memory; up to 1M tokens depending on the model, 200k for other models including Claude Sonnet 4.5; everything in the request and the output counts; input alone over the window returns a 400 invalid_request_error, prompt is too long, on every model; chat interfaces such as claude.ai can manage the window on a rolling first in, first out basis; context rot; use the token counting API to estimate usage before sending
